The West Indian chiton Chiton tuberculatus is a common inhabitant of intertidal rocky shores throughout the Caribbean, where it grazes on algal films. Field surveys indicate that the species attains a maximum shell length of 10 centimeters [Li = 10 centimeters], a value that represents the upper limit of its asymptotic growth under favorable conditions in exposed habitats. The wet weight at birth, based on the size of fertilized ova, is approximately 0.0000042 grams [Wwb = approximately 0.0000042 grams], a minuscule size reflecting the minute egg diameter typical of many polyplacophorans that broadcast spawn and invest minimally in each individual offspring. Upon hatching, the free-swimming veliger larva undergoes a brief planktonic phase before reaching metamorphic competence. At metamorphosis, the body mass is recorded at around 0.0000043 grams , a value that remains nearly identical to the birth mass and indicates that the short larval period involves minimal somatic growth. Settlement and substratum attachment follow within hours of hatching, leading to the rapid reorganisation of the body plan as the juvenile assumes the adult benthic form.

Reproductive effort in Chiton tuberculatus has been estimated from size-corrected comparisons with related species. Females produce roughly 1,780 eggs per individual annually [Ri = roughly 1,780 eggs per individual annually] when evaluated at a stable water temperature of 10 °C [T = 10 °C], a regime that reflects the cooler winter conditions in parts of its subtropical range. Given that spawning is a single seasonal event per year [F_R_i = single seasonal event per year], the annual fecundity directly translates to the daily maximum reproduction rate under these thermal conditions. The onset of gonadal activity and the first successful spawning event occur only after individuals have attained a body length of 2.5 centimeters [Lp = 2.5 centimeters], a size threshold indicating the completion of essential somatic growth before the allocation of resources to gamete production. Smaller juveniles below that size threshold are entirely somatic in their growth trajectory and are never observed to be gravid.

The ultimate wet weight of a fully grown adult of Chiton tuberculatus reaches approximately 120 grams [Wwi = approximately 120 grams], a body mass comparable to that of other large chitons such as Katharina tunicata, which occupies a similar ecological niche in the North Pacific. This substantial mass is supported by the expansion of the thickened girdle and the robust articulamentum of the shell valves. This dramatic size increase is evident from the initial mass of a new egg, which is 0.0000042 grams [Wwb = 0.0000042 grams], meaning the adult is over seven orders of magnitude heavier. The post-metamorphic juvenile, upon first settling, has an estimated wet weight of 4.3 millionths of a gram , which is essentially indistinguishable from the egg mass. This observation underscores the fact that all substantial growth in this species occurs after larval settlement, during the benthic juvenile and adult phases.

Longevity records for Chiton tuberculatus, derived from mark-recapture studies and growth-ring analysis of the shell valves, suggest that the maximum lifespan approaches 12 years [am = 12 years] under field conditions at a mean water temperature of 10 °C [T = 10 °C]. This comparatively long life span is likely an underestimate given that growth may continue at a very slow rate beyond the twelfth year, but few specimens older than this have been collected. The species therefore exhibits a life-history strategy characterized by slow somatic growth, a late onset of female reproduction at a shell length of 2.5 centimeters [Lp = 2.5 centimeters], and a protracted reproductive window spanning many seasons. The metric of ultimate length, measured at 10 centimeters [Li = 10 centimeters], is attained only by the oldest and largest individuals in a population and typically coincides with the peak of their reproductive output. Field-collected animals approaching this maximum length are often heavily encrusted with epibionts, indicating considerable time spent attached to the substrate.

Comparative analysis of body proportions within the Polyplacophora reveals that the 2.5 centimeters [Lp = 2.5 centimeters] length at puberty for Chiton tuberculatus, which represents roughly a quarter of its ultimate length, is a typical scaling relationship among chiton species of moderate to large body size. The asymptotic wet weight of 120 grams [Wwi = 120 grams] is achieved only near the end of the animal's 12-year maximum life span (12 years) [am = 12 years] at 10 °C [T = 10 °C], suggesting that weight gain decelerates sharply after maturity. By contrast, the larval stages are extraordinarily brief, with the wet weight at metamorphosis remaining at just over 0.0000043 grams , a value that underscores the paucity of feeding opportunities in the plankton. This reproductive strategy, which relies on the release of many small eggs, each with a mass of 0.0000042 grams [Wwb = 0.0000042 grams], and the subsequent development of planktotrophic larvae, is consistent with the opportunistic feeding ecology of this intertidal grazer. The reproductive output, estimated at roughly 1,780 eggs per year [Ri = roughly 1,780 eggs per year] during a single seasonal spawning event per year [F_R_i = single seasonal spawning event per year] at 10 °C [T = 10 °C], aligns well with fecundity values observed in other warm-water chiton species.
